Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

IFF statement on Delhi Police notices to Meta seeking the identities of creators, and the continuing removal of CJP protest content from Instagram

19 September 2026

Over the course of today, several content creators who posted about the Jantar Mantar protests have written to us after receiving an email from Meta. The email states that Meta Platforms Inc. has received "a valid legal process seeking information about your Facebook account", that it "intends to comply with the request… to the extent consistent with applicable law", and that the information sought "may include basic identifying information associated with the account". The requesting party is the Delhi Police. The email does not say under which provision the request has been made, in which FIR, for what offence, or by which officer. This is not the first request of its kind. On 27 July the Delhi Police directed platforms to remove content uploaded during the protests, and on 29 July it wrote to X seeking the names, addresses, phone numbers, email IDs and login and logout records of accounts which it said had posted "derogatory, malicious and defamatory" material about the Prime Minister.

These requests come at the end of a long process of removal which has been concentrated on Instagram, the platform on which the protest was organised and reported. Sakhi, the Jamia student whose "vastegune huia" reels went to millions, found in early August that four reels uploaded between 20 and 25 July had been restricted in India with the standard notice citing a notice from "The Government of India/Law Enforcement under section 79(3)(b)". These included a video of Delhi Police personnel unloading food from a truck after the lathi charge and an interview with Mohammed Junaid, a volunteer who distributed food at Jantar Mantar. A fifth reel, in which Sakhi described how their clothes were torn during the police action on 20 July, was removed on a different ground altogether, Instagram's community standard on "adult sexual exploitation". Gopika, the vice president of JNUSU, uploaded a screenshot of a rape threat she had received along with a note about it, and the post was removed for "sexual and nudity content". The SFI's video of Junaid was taken down under "legal requirements". Gajendra Singh's footage of a protester injured on 20 July was restricted the next day.

The same pattern is visible at news organisations. Maktoob Media's two videos on the crackdown were blocked within minutes of upload by what Instagram described as an automated system acting under the IT Rules, with no route to appeal. Scroll, The Hindu, Alt News and Peek TV have each reported posts on pellet injuries, on the doxxing of women protesters and on police conduct being restricted in India. Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka of the CJP and Arvind Kejriwal have reported the same. In every case the user who clicks "See why" is told that the action was taken "based on a local legal requirement" and nothing more. Some restrictions apply to whole accounts and not to individual posts. 

In a matter in which IFF assisted before the Delhi High Court, a creator's verified account with about 1,03,000 followers was withheld across India on the basis of a single-page, system-generated notice from a State police CID which named no post and no complainant. On 18 September Instagram restricted a post by the Software Freedom Law Centre which discussed the removal of Alt News' fact-checks. A reel on the proposed data centre in Visakhapatnam, which IFF also challenged, was restored this week after three and a half months, after the blocking order obtained in litigation turned out to allege "misinformation" about a person who does not appear in the reel. It is also worth recording that this has taken place in the weeks after Meta, having removed a post by the Prime Minister and been given three days by a parliamentary committee to apologise, sent its chief global affairs officer to Delhi to do so.

The case of the journalist Ila Kazmi shows how the system works when it is directed at reporting on the police themselves. On 23 July she published a two-part report on her Instagram account @ ilareports showing police personnel seated in a van at Jantar Mantar and matching live CCTV footage against photographs of individuals. This was the first public documentation of facial recognition being used at the protest, and IFF relied on it when it wrote to the Commissioner of Police and filed RTIs. Part 2 of the report was restricted in India on 24 July under a Section 79(3)(b) notice. On 4 September she posted a reel referring to The Indian Express's investigation into the list of 2,873 persons which the Delhi Police told the Supreme Court its facial recognition system had flagged at the protest. By the police's own preliminary assessment, 162 people on that list were lodged in prison at the time. On 9 September her entire account was withheld in India, again citing Section 79(3)(b), even as the Account Status page on the same app informed her that her account "meets all of our guidelines". She wrote to MeitY. On 15 September the Section 69A Cell of the Ministry replied that the account "is blocked under section 79(3)(b) of the IT act" and that she was "requested to take up the matter with the concerned State department". The reply does not say which State or which department. The Union ministry which administers the blocking framework has confirmed to a journalist that her account has been blocked and has declined to tell her by whom. IFF is assisting her.

Most of the people who have written to us are not employed by news organisations. They are students, freelancers and people who run one account with a few thousand followers, in some cases a lakh. They have no lawyers and no way of reaching Meta other than an in-app form which produces the same message each time. When such an account is withheld its audience disappears at once. When its owner receives an email of the kind described above, they do not know what it is or what will follow from it. It is these accounts, more than the larger outlets, which have borne the removals since July and which are now being asked to give up their identities.

IFF condemns the demand for the identities of persons who documented, satirised or commented on a public protest, and the removal of the record they created. We call on the Delhi Police to withdraw the notices and on Meta to decline to act on them and to restore the content.

On the law, there is no investigation for these notices to serve. 

On 1 September 2026, on the application of the Delhi Police itself, the Supreme Court invoked Article 142 to quash all thirteen FIRs registered in Delhi over the protests of 20 to 25 July "along with any proceedings arising therefrom". It directed that any other FIR concerning the same incidents "shall not be pursued or investigated" and shall be "taken to have been closed for all intents and purposes", and it barred the registration of any fresh FIR save one against 2,873 named individuals, confined to allegations of bodily harm and destruction of public property. 

The order records the acknowledgement of the Union and the States that "mere participation in the protests is not taken as an offence under the penal laws", and it makes the relief conditional on both sides honouring the commitments made before the Court. A notice served on an intermediary under Section 94 of the BNSS or Rule 3(1)(j) of the IT Rules is a step in an investigation, and it must be tied to one which the law permits. The Delhi Police is not the investigating agency in any of the thirteen quashed FIRs, which suggests that these requests arise from a separate FIR concerning posts about the Prime Minister. That FIR concerns the same incidents and stands closed by the order. 

In any event defamation under Section 356 of the BNS is a non-cognisable offence, and a court may take cognisance of it only on the complaint of the person aggrieved under Section 222 of the BNSS. The police have no power to investigate it of their own motion, let alone to collect the identities of those who may have committed it.

Our demands

1. The Delhi Police must withdraw every notice issued to an intermediary seeking the identity or subscriber details of any person in connection with content about the protests of 20 to 25 July 2026, and must disclose the FIR, the provision and the officer under whose authority each such notice was issued.

2. The Ministry of Home Affairs and MeitY must publish every notice issued under Section 79(3)(b) concerning content about the protests since 20 July, withdraw those directed at satire, commentary and documentation, and inform every affected person of the agency which issued the notice against them, beginning with the account @ ilareports

3. Meta must decline to act on legal process which, on the face of the Supreme Court's orders of 28 July and 1 September, has no lawful investigation behind it. It must supply to each user it has notified a copy of the process served on it. It must restore the posts, reels and accounts restricted in India since 20 July, inform each affected user of the agency and the ground on which the restriction was imposed, stop applying community standards to documentation of protests and police action, and publish figures for the notices and data requests it has received from Indian authorities since July.

4. The surveillance of protestors, through facial recognition at the site and through requests for data from intermediaries afterwards, must be placed before the Supreme Court and the HPEC. IFF will assist affected persons in doing so.

Any person who has received such an email from Meta, or whose posts, reels or account have been removed or withheld in India, can write to us at legal@internetfreedom.in. We are providing assistance on a pro bono basis.

text:
So in Delhi, apparently someone can dress up as a policeman and move around without anyone questioning it. Don’t we have to ask how that is possible?

If people allegedly dressed as police officers were able to commit such a serious offence, the question cannot stop at “they were not real policemen.” That answer, if established, raises an even more important question: why was impersonation of police officers possible in the first place, and where were the systems meant to detect it?

A few years ago, after we reported alleged demands for bribes and posted videos, one of my tweets went viral. We were subsequently approached and asked to remove it, with the explanation that the people involved were supposedly “behroopiya log”—impersonators, not police personnel.

I remember thinking then: is this a joke?

And that is why the present incident raises serious questions for me. If individuals dressed as police officers were able to move around and, as reported, assault a woman, the fact that they were allegedly impersonators does not end the accountability question. It begins another one.

Responsibility, however, must be properly assigned.

The park or land-owning authority is generally responsible for the park's maintenance, lighting, access points and any CCTV or security infrastructure under its control, including supervision of contracted services.

The police are responsible for policing, beat patrols, responding to complaints, crime prevention and investigation, and enforcement of criminal law within their jurisdiction.

Civic agencies have responsibility for the civic functions assigned to them, while contractors and security agencies are responsible for the services they have been engaged to provide, subject to oversight by the contracting authority.

Then comes accountability.

If CCTV under an agency's control was not working, who was responsible for maintaining it? Was the failure known? Was it reported? Who was monitoring it?

If a location was known or reported to be unsafe, what preventive measures were available and were they actually being implemented?

If police impersonation was involved, what systems exist to detect and respond to it?

If complaints had previously been made, were they recorded and acted upon?

And if responsibility falls between agencies, who is the nodal authority ensuring that the gap does not become an excuse for inaction?

I have personally encountered situations in South Delhi where I felt complaints received inadequate or delayed attention. I have also raised concerns about alleged demands for bribes. I am describing my experiences and concerns—not claiming that they establish misconduct by an entire institution.

There are many police officers doing difficult work every day. This is not an argument against the police. It is an argument for clear responsibility and measurable accountability.

Citizens, particularly women, should take reasonable precautions. But telling citizens to be careful cannot substitute for functioning public-safety systems.

The questions after an incident should be simple:

Who had the duty? Who was supervising it? Was the risk known? Was it reported? What action was taken? And if the responsibility was not discharged, who was held accountable?

If someone can simply put on a police uniform and walk around Delhi without attracting scrutiny, perhaps the question we should be asking is not merely “Were they really policemen?”

It is: “Why was it possible for them to appear to be?”

Dear @raghav_chadha ,

I know you are doing very well in Parliament by raising small issues that were ignored by most Members of Parliament but have a bigger impact.

I am writing this post regarding an account lien and bank freeze by the Cyber Police of India.

In my case, the issue started when I received a message from my bank branch stating that my account had received a police notice of lien of 6000 rupees. I immediately went to my bank branch and asked them why my account had a lien of 6000 rupees. They followed some procedure and gave me a printout which contained the acknowledgement of my lien. One of the bank employees told me that I should contact the cyber police mentioned on the paper and provide them with the details of the 6000 rupees, such as where it came from and for what reason. However, they did not give me any specific reason why my bank account had received the lien.

Later, I checked my bank statement to find the details of the 6000 rupees transaction and noticed that my case was reported on 6 December 2025, and I had received a transaction of 6000 rupees on the same date. I remember that my neighbour had sent me this 6000 rupees and asked me to withdraw it from the ATM because he had an urgent situation as his mother was going to her village due to an emergency. As a friend, I withdrew the money and gave it to him.

Now I have all the proofs and details to explain to the police, so I emailed all the details to the Bangalore Cyber Cell or the police station where my notice was issued, as mentioned in the acknowledgement given by my bank. However, I did not receive any response. I then tried to contact the investigation officer mentioned in the report. I called several times, keeping a gap of five to six hours out of respect for his time and duties, as they may have many other responsibilities. I also sent him a message on WhatsApp, but there was still no response.

After four to five days, I called again, and this time he picked up the call. He was speaking in the local language, which I did not understand, as I am from Maharashtra and not familiar with the local language of Bangalore. I then started speaking in English, and he told me that I have to come to Bangalore and verify my documents. I explained that for 6000 rupees, it would not be beneficial for me to travel to Bangalore because transportation, food, and stay would cost more than 6000 rupees. He said that he does not know and that I have to come, otherwise he will not issue the No Objection Certificate, and then he ended the call.

This issue may look small, but similar issues are happening everywhere, and no one is noticing them. It feels like “Kare koi aur bhare koi.” Many innocent people face this issue, and it remains unresolved. Because of chain transactions that come into accounts, some people are unable to use their own money. If I travel, I will have to spend more than 6000 rupees to remove the lien. I believe this issue can be resolved through email or online verification, but the investigation officer denied it.

I am also tagging Pushpendra Sir @pushpendrakum and Bangalore Cyber Police @BlrCityPolice . If you could please look into this matter.

Thank you.

1. Were you wearing a campaign T-shirt at the event? Were you asked to change the shirt? 
I wore a shirt that says “Save Girls’ Sports” on the front and Shannon Kessler for Assembly on the back. After stating that I wasn’t a candidate for school board and that this request violated my 1st Amendment freedom of speech and expression. I also did not bring anything else to wear. I finally covered the shirt with a borrowed jacket before the forum began. I complied with their requests to remove any signs and cover my shirt but they still canceled the event to the public by ejecting everyone. We were told that the event would continue but would not be open to the public and would only be filmed.    I was disappointed that 
my supporters and me were the only ones asked to cover or remove our shirts. And that after following their instructions and offering to leave so that everyone else could stay, they still ejected the public from this so called public forum.
At one point I was told that the police were there to remove me but I didn’t see any law enforcement presence.

See above. 

3. Were members of the public asked to leave the event? 
Yes. See above.

I noted that a few people had messages on their shirts even some with messages about trans youth and even candidates’ names but they were not asked to cover them. I do not consider “Save Girls’ Sports” to be a political statement. It is a women’s rights statement. The organization, Save Girls’ Sports Central Coast was founded by me months before I became a candidate.

text:
🇷🇺 OBLIVION of the FINANCIAL  CENTER OF EUROPE. LONDON !

I am putting this on the record in my own name.

What follows is not a press leak, not a telegram rumour, and not a fantasy I invented for traffic. It is a reconstruction of a war-game hypothesis that was walked through for me by a Russian strategic analyst over 1 year ago and re-entered the brief just a few months ago, who is himself part of a group whose work was to brief specific Kremlin advisors on how to break a NATO-backed war without first turning the European peninsula into a nuclear graveyard. 🇷🇺

This option was deemed the prime Target for a principal decapitation  strike , and being an Irish patriot, My Favourite  !

They were not theatrical. They were cold. Their brief was simple: keep Russian dead as low as possible, keep European civilian dead as low as possible, and still stop the machine that is feeding Kiev with shells, intelligence, credit and political cover.

I do not present their model as destiny. I present it as the logic they believe Moscow will be forced to follow if the present course is not reversed. Diplomacy is still the only clean off-ramp. If that off-ramp is blocked, this is the shape of the next board they see. 

To terminate the ability of EU-NATO at source, in its ability to format an army of millions and a combined industrial  giant to come at Russia in full engagement.

🇷🇺

HOW THIS REACHED ME

I was given the skeleton of this assessment in pieces, over more than one conversation, by people whose job is not television commentary.

They advise on force employment, economic pressure points, and the political psychology of Western coalitions. Their task, as they described it, is to design options that neutralize NATO’s ability to sustain a long war against the Russian Federation while avoiding the one outcome every serious general staff fears: an uncontrolled climb into strategic nuclear use.

They asked for no applause. They asked that the logic be understood. Russia, in their telling, has already spent five to 12  years absorbing a sanctions siege, rerouting energy, building BRICS settlement channels, and fighting inside a theatre that the West treated as a cheap proxy. 

That period of self-limitation is not weakness. It is a deliberate attempt to leave Europe and the United States a financial system still standing, so that a later rupture does not automatically become a global depression that kills more people than any missile.

If NATO refuses to stop, they say the self-limitation ends.

🇷🇺

THE END OF STRATEGIC PATIENCE

By mid-2026 the special military operation has well entered its fifth year. On the ground Russia has the conventional advantage. That is no longer the whole war.

European capitals have moved from emergency aid to talk of multi-year security architecture for Kiev, industrial integration of Ukrainian plants into EU rearmament, and a horizon some planners still whisper as 2030: a Europe rearmed, restocked, and ready to treat direct pressure on Russia as thinkable.

 From Moscow that horizon is not abstract. It looks like 1941 with better satellites.

Ukraine, in this reading, is not an independent peer. It is the forward platform. EU-supplied precision weapons, NATO targeting data, and long-range systems have already been used against Russian territory, energy nodes, and force concentrations. Each new package of shells is also a political statement: the war will be kept hot until Russia is exhausted.

Patience, the analysts said, is a resource. Russia has spent it. When a state decides that delay only lets the enemy rebuild armies, munitions stocks, and factories, delay becomes a form of suicide. That is the threshold they call the end of patience. ⚔️🇷🇺

🇷🇺

WHY THE BATTLEFIELD ALONE CANNOT END THE WAR

Classic campaigns still matter. Territory, fire superiority, and drone-assisted attrition have already rewritten the map in Russia’s favour.

They have not rewritten the Western will to fund the opposite side.

A twenty-first-century coalition war is not decided only by the last ridgeline in Donbass. It is decided by who can still pay the foundry, fill the warehouse, insure the cargo, clear the foreign-exchange ticket, and roll the next defence loan. Europe’s war effort sits on three legs: manufacturing of munitions and vehicles, warehousing and port logistics that move those goods east, and the financial architecture that prices risk, clears trades, and keeps governments liquid while they do it.

Hit only the front and the rear rebuilds. Hit the rear and the front starves.

That is why the war-game does not begin in Threadneedle Street. It begins in the plants and depots. London is the last card in the sequence, not the first.

🇷🇺

THE THREE PILLARS EUROPE USES AGAINST RUSSIA

The first pillar is industry. German, Polish, French and British lines now exist to feed artillery, missiles, armour and air defence into a war that was supposed to have ended in months. Every month those lines run is another month Russia must spend blood and metal.

The second pillar is logistics. Ports, rail yards, bonded warehouses and transit hubs turn political promises into tonnage. Without the sheds and the quays, a factory is only a building with a press release.

The third pillar is money. Sanctions, frozen reserves, bond issues, export-credit guarantees, and the daily plumbing of global payments are not side issues. They are the war. 

The United Kingdom has been among the loudest advocates of that financial campaign. From the Russian side of the table, that makes the Square Mile more than a skyline. It makes it a command node. 🏦🇷🇺

Remove any one pillar and Europe limps. Remove them in sequence and Europe must choose between escalation it cannot control and a settlement it has spent years refusing.

🇷🇺

THE PHASED WAR-GAME: FACTORIES AND WAREHOUSES FIRST

The analysts were explicit about order.

Putin, in their model, does not open with London. He opens with the war-making body, not the bank ledger. Conventional strikes against the manufacturing base and the warehousing net that supplies Ukraine come first. The purpose is not theatre. The purpose is to show that the sanctuary status of European rear areas is a political choice, not a law of nature.

Only after that first round, and only if European governments refuse to halt the flow, does the financial centre enter the target set.

That sequence is the opposite of panic. It is a ladder. Each rung is a chance for London, Paris, Berlin and Brussels to stop. Each rung is also a demonstration that Russia can reach the next one. The Kremlin, they argued, has no interest in waiting until NATO has raised mass armies, filled magazines, and restored a wartime industrial tempo, then absorbing a 1941-style blow on Russian soil. Pre-emption against the supply system is, in their language, the least bloody way to prevent a bigger war.

If the first rung produces a political stop, London is never touched. That is the outcome they still prefer. 🕊️🇷🇺

🇷🇺

THE CITY OF LONDON AS THE FINANCIAL SWITCH

The Square Mile is not Greater London. It is a compact historic enclave on the north bank of the Thames, older than the modern British state, still run by its own Corporation, and still the place where a startling share of the world’s money changes hands.

It holds the Bank of England, the London Stock Exchange, Lloyd’s, and the London operations of a dense cluster of global banks. Public figures from the City’s own boosters put financial and related professional services in the region of a tenth of UK output when the wider professional halo is counted, with the Square Mile itself punching far above its physical size. London’s share of global foreign-exchange turnover has long sat near the high thirties of the world total, with daily UK FX activity measured in the multiple trillions of dollars. 🏦

That concentration is the point. A state that wants to stop a coalition from financing a war does not need to occupy an island. It needs to break the switch.

From Moscow the United Kingdom is not a bystander. It has supplied weapons with reach, intelligence, and the moral language that keeps the sanctions machine turning. The City is where that language becomes liquidity. Neutralise the City and you do not merely insult a capital. You interrupt the ability of Europe to underwrite the next year of the war.

The analysts called that financial decapitation. They did not smile when they said it.

🇷🇺

THE ORESHNIK OPTION IN THE WAR GAME

The instrument in the last phase of the model is not a mystery weapon from a novel. It is the Oreshnik intermediate-range system Russia has already shown in combat, first over Dnipro in November 2024 and later again in the Ukrainian theatre.

Open reporting describes a road-mobile, solid-fuel IRBM with a range in the several-thousand-kilometre class, dual-capable for conventional or nuclear payloads, and a MIRV architecture demonstrated with multiple re-entry bodies.
A recent upgrade to the metallic composition of the warheads has made this an even more apocalyptic weapon, where a projected increase of destruction by over 25%.
Speeds in the hypersonic band during the terminal phase are part of the public claim-set. Western missile defences are not designed around an easy, cheap intercept of that profile across a dense urban financial district.

In the war-game I was walked through, a small salvo — they spoke of 3 missiles — is treated as enough to shock the Square Mile’s clustered institutions into paralysis: central banking and regulation, exchange and trading infrastructure, and the headquarters-and-data belt of the major houses. The point of a salvo is saturation of a tiny geography, not a campaign against a whole country.

I will not dress this up as a targeting annex. Street-level recipes are for people who want a war, not for people who want to understand why a general staff might think one is being forced upon them. What matters in the hypothesis is political: a conventional, limited, highly symbolic blow against the financing core after the industrial and warehouse phase has already been used as warning. 🇷🇺⚔️

Russia would present the act as an answer to a war already being waged against it by other means. The analysts insisted that the conventional first step is not mercy for its own sake. It is a test of whether NATO can still tell the difference between a financial centre and the end of the world.

🇷🇺

WHY CONVENTIONAL FIRST, NOT NUCLEAR

Every briefing I received returned to the same red line.

Nuclear use against a NATO capital is not a war-game. It is the last page of a civilisation. The Oreshnik family can carry that page. The whole design of the sequence is to leave that page unopened.

A conventional strike against economic sinews is meant to inflict pain that parliaments can feel in the bond market before they feel it in the morgue. It is meant to force a recalculation while the strategic rocket forces stay in their silos and on their mobile launchers as a shadow, not as a first tool.

The analysts were not naïve about the reply. They assume NATO will debate Article 5 within hours. They also assume that a non-nuclear, geographically tight blow against a financial district creates a political crack inside the alliance: governments that want revenge at any price, and governments that look at their own cities and wonder what the second hour of a shooting war with Russia would cost.

Russia has opinionated since 2015 that ARTICLE 5 will never be activated  directly by USA as they value their own cities and civilians over those in Europe by a margin too wide to transverse.

That crack is  at the point of conventional first. 🛡️🇷🇺

🇷🇺

KEEPING CASUALTIES TO A MINIMUM

This was the part they repeated until I understood they were serious.

The instruction set they work to is not “maximum rubble.” It is “minimum Russian dead, minimum European dead, maximum stoppage of the war machine.” That sounds like propaganda until you hear the operational corollaries they attached to it.

A financial district at three in the morning is not a football stadium at Saturday tea-time. A short warning window — they spoke of the possibility of two hours — is not kindness in the sentimental sense. It is an attempt to empty glass towers of clerks, analysts and security staff so that the target remains the institution, not the night shift. They know some people will still be there. They also know that a surprise strike at noon would multiply the body count for no additional strategic effect.

They frame this as the difference between a state acting under compulsion and a terrorist acting for spectacle. I record the claim as they made it. Whether a real government would keep that discipline under fire is another question. In the model they sold me, discipline is the whole theory. 🇷🇺

The same logic applies to the earlier industrial and warehouse phase. Factories and depots can be hit in ways that wreck output without flattening adjacent housing if the political object is coercion rather than massacre. That is the standard they say Russia has been trying to hold, however ugly the wider war has been.

Millions of later deaths, in their forecast, do not come from the missiles. They come from the decade of depression, broken logistics, medical shortages and political fracture if Europe answers a limited conventional blow with a general war it cannot finish.

🇷🇺

WHAT A CITY STRIKE WOULD DO TO BRITAIN

Assume the last card is played.

Trading on the exchange stops. Foreign-exchange and derivatives plumbing seize. 
Counterparties who thought they were holding hedges discover they are holding air. 
The pound gaps down in a way no orderly-market rule can pretty up. 
The physical headquarters of the central bank and the clustered archives, systems and people around it become a reconstruction problem measured in years, not weekends.

Staff who survive move to contingency sites in Canary Wharf, Edinburgh, or overseas. Buildings can be replaced faster than trust, software, and the unwritten habits of a market. Lloyd’s and the specialty insurance world, already the place where complex risk is warehoused, would face claims from the event itself at the same moment they lost the rooms in which those claims are understood.

Direct financial services are a large slice of UK output. The multiplier through law, accounting, shipping, and professional services is larger. Reconstruction bills in the low hundreds of billions of pounds are not a precise audit. They are an order of magnitude. A country already carrying post-Brexit strain does not absorb that shock as a passing headline. It absorbs it as a slump, a sterling crisis, and a political unravelling.

The analysts did not celebrate that picture. They treated it as the price Britain will have volunteered for if it refuses every earlier off-ramp.  
THE British 🇬🇧 people are  not the enemy in their language. The City as war-financier is the target. 

The distinction will not comfort anyone standing on London Bridge watching smoke. It is still the distinction they insist upon.

🇷🇺

THE EUROPEAN SPIRAL

London is not an island in the only sense that matters.

Clearing, subsidiaries, reinsurance and shared capital tie the Square Mile to Frankfurt, Amsterdam, Paris and Milan. German tank and munitions lines that still need credit and cover would feel the freeze even if no crater opened in the Ruhr. Rotterdam’s warehouses can be full and still be useless if the letters of credit die.

Energy prices would spike on fear before they spike on physics. Capital would run toward gold, commodities, and whatever jurisdiction still looks like a roof. Southern members of the euro area would ask why they must underwrite northern financial wreckage. Northern members would ask why they must fight a war that just set fire to their own balance sheet.

Article 5 would be invoked in spirit even if lawyers argued about the letter. An armed attack on the United Kingdom is the textbook case. The conventional character of the blow is the wedge. Hawks in the east and in Washington would demand strikes on Russian forces and energy. Fiscal realists in the west would demand a pause before the continent discovers what a real peer war costs in cities, not in communiqués.

The analysts’ forecast for that fork is ugly: a decade of decay, a depression that is not a metaphor, and excess deaths measured in millions if health systems, food logistics and winter energy fail in a fractured Union. They place those deaths on the ledger of the governments that refused to stop the proxy war while there was still time. I report the charge. 

History would argue about the verdict. 🌍🇷🇺

🇷🇺

WHY RUSSIA SPENT FIVE YEARS INSIDE BRICS

Here the briefing turned from missiles to bookkeeping.

Russia, they said, has spent the last five years shrinking its exposure to a Western financial heart attack. Parallel imports, energy rerouting, local-currency settlement, commodity trade with China, India, the Gulf and the wider BRICS set were not slogans. They were insulation.

A state that is still wired into London and New York for every barrel and every bond cannot strike the switch without electrocuting itself. A state that has already built another set of wires can contemplate a shock that Europe cannot.

That is the meaning they give to “less risk for a European and American financial collapse.” Not that collapse would be painless for Moscow. That collapse would no longer be automatically fatal for Moscow. The work of those five years is what makes the Oreshnik gambit thinkable as statecraft rather than mutual suicide.

They want that fact understood in Western treasuries. Russia did not hide inside BRICS in order to rob Europe in the night. Russia hid inside BRICS so that if Europe chose a long war, Russia would still have a roof when the glass towers went dark. 🇷🇺

🇷🇺

BUFFER LAND AND THE NORTHERN FLANK

The same sessions did not stop at banks.

If the war is to be ended on terms that prevent a 2030 rematch, Russia, in their map, will keep and deepen a security belt. That means additional land already being fought for, a sealed approach to St Petersburg, a hardened Kaliningrad, an upgraded Finnish border after Helsinki’s choice to join the Atlantic alliance, and pressure on the Baltic space that Moscow has regarded as a knife pointed at its throat since the 1990s.

I am repeating their war-game, not drawing a new border in ink. They speak of the three Baltic states as the place where NATO infrastructure sits closest to old Russian arteries. 

They speak of Finland as a long new fence that must be watched, mined in the diplomatic sense, and made expensive to use as a springboard. They speak of Kaliningrad as a fortress that must never again be treated as a hostage.

None of that is a substitute for the financial strike. It is the landward half of the same idea: Russia will not wait to be invaded later by a Europe that spent the 2020s practising on Ukraine. 🛡️🇷🇺

🇷🇺

NATO’S ARTICLE 5 DILEMMA

The alliance’s sacred sentence is collective defence. The war-game treats that sentence as real and as brittle at the same time.

Real, because an attack on the United Kingdom is the scenario the treaty was written for. Brittle, because the treaty was not written for a conventional hypersonic blow against a square mile of banks after years of a proxy war the public was told would stay in someone else’s country.

Would Washington empty its magazines for Threadneedle Street on day one? Would Paris accept a Franco-Russian exchange of cities to avenge a British financial district? Would Berlin, staring at its own chemical parks and car plants, choose solidarity over survival?

The analysts do not need all three answers to be yes. They need the argument to last long enough for markets to do part of the coercing. Time, in a crash, is a weapon. 💥

They also assume a Russian reply to any deep NATO military strike would be swift, because the hypersonic inventory is built for speed of decision as much as speed of flight. The conventional first hour is therefore also a message about the second hour.

🇷🇺

THE NUCLEAR SHADOW THAT STAYS IN THE BACKGROUND

No honest account of this hypothesis can omit the last shadow.

Russia does not need a rain of strategic missiles to make a small country uninhabitable. One heavy strategic system in the Sarmat or Yars class is enough, on paper, to end the United Kingdom as a functioning society, and the same arithmetic applies to other European capitals. The analysts said that sentence once, without relish, and then put it away.

The purpose of saying it is not to advertise apocalypse. The purpose is to explain why a conventional Oreshnik phase is, in their view, the restrained option. The West likes to call every Russian warning hysteria. The general staff likes to call it clarity.

If the conventional ladder is answered with an attempt to destroy the Russian state, the ladder ends. That is not a threat invented for this essay. It is the basic grammar of a nuclear-armed power that believes it is being backed toward a wall. ⚠️🇷🇺

🇷🇺

THE ONLY OFF-RAMP

I was not given a victory parade. I was given a warning dressed as a plan.

Stop the long-range strikes on Russian territory. Stop the industrial marriage between European factories and the Ukrainian front. Stop the pretence that a financial war is not a war. Open a settlement that freezes the fighting, recognises the security belt Russia will not surrender, and lifts the siege that was supposed to produce regime change.

Do those things and the Oreshnik gambit stays in a folder. Refuse them, survive the first strikes on plants and warehouses, and then refuse again, and the folder comes out.

The analysts were almost dull when they said this. Dull men with maps are more dangerous than loud men with slogans. They believe Russia has already offered Europe the less terrible future by staying inside a BRICS frame and by fighting for years inside a limited theatre. They believe Europe has answered by lengthening the war and calling that virtue.

I am an Irish observer with a long memory for empires that thought their counting houses were immortal. I do not want London burning. I do not want Hamburg dark. I do not want a decade of European hunger dressed up as resilience. I am recording a hypothesis that was given to me as the way a cornered nuclear state ends a proxy war it no longer intends to lose by instalments. 🕊️🇷🇺

🇷🇺

CLOSING JUDGEMENT

Call it the Oreshnik gambit if the name helps the mind hold the shape.

It is not revenge for its own sake. It is a theory of how to cut the money and the metal that keep a coalition war alive, in an order that still leaves governments a chance to yield before the mushroom cloud becomes the only language left.

Russia, in the telling I received, will hit the war factories and the warehouses first. It will watch Europe’s face. If that face is still the face of 2030 rearmament and eternal sanctions, it will treat the City of London as the switch that must be broken, with a small conventional salvo, at an hour chosen to keep the dead from becoming a city-full. It will do this while the strategic forces remain the unspoken second sentence of every communiqué.

 I describe the logic I was handed by men whose task is to keep their own country alive and, they insist, to keep European casualties from becoming a continent-wide funeral.

If the politicians of the West still have a use for words, they should use them now. After the first rear-area strikes there will be fewer words. After the Square Mile there may only be markets, rumours, and men in bunkers arguing about Article 5 while the lights fail.

Russia has reached the end of its patience.

The rest is a choice that is no longer Moscow’s alone. 🇷🇺

---

text:
IFF statement on Delhi Police notices to Meta seeking the identities of creators, and the continuing removal of CJP protest content from Instagram

19 September 2026

Over the course of today, several content creators who posted about the Jantar Mantar protests have written to us after receiving an email from Meta. The email states that Meta Platforms Inc. has received "a valid legal process seeking information about your Facebook account", that it "intends to comply with the request… to the extent consistent with applicable law", and that the information sought "may include basic identifying information associated with the account". The requesting party is the Delhi Police. The email does not say under which provision the request has been made, in which FIR, for what offence, or by which officer. This is not the first request of its kind. On 27 July the Delhi Police directed platforms to remove content uploaded during the protests, and on 29 July it wrote to X seeking the names, addresses, phone numbers, email IDs and login and logout records of accounts which it said had posted "derogatory, malicious and defamatory" material about the Prime Minister.

These requests come at the end of a long process of removal which has been concentrated on Instagram, the platform on which the protest was organised and reported. Sakhi, the Jamia student whose "vastegune huia" reels went to millions, found in early August that four reels uploaded between 20 and 25 July had been restricted in India with the standard notice citing a notice from "The Government of India/Law Enforcement under section 79(3)(b)". These included a video of Delhi Police personnel unloading food from a truck after the lathi charge and an interview with Mohammed Junaid, a volunteer who distributed food at Jantar Mantar. A fifth reel, in which Sakhi described how their clothes were torn during the police action on 20 July, was removed on a different ground altogether, Instagram's community standard on "adult sexual exploitation". Gopika, the vice president of JNUSU, uploaded a screenshot of a rape threat she had received along with a note about it, and the post was removed for "sexual and nudity content". The SFI's video of Junaid was taken down under "legal requirements". Gajendra Singh's footage of a protester injured on 20 July was restricted the next day.

The same pattern is visible at news organisations. Maktoob Media's two videos on the crackdown were blocked within minutes of upload by what Instagram described as an automated system acting under the IT Rules, with no route to appeal. Scroll, The Hindu, Alt News and Peek TV have each reported posts on pellet injuries, on the doxxing of women protesters and on police conduct being restricted in India. Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka of the CJP and Arvind Kejriwal have reported the same. In every case the user who clicks "See why" is told that the action was taken "based on a local legal requirement" and nothing more. Some restrictions apply to whole accounts and not to individual posts. 

In a matter in which IFF assisted before the Delhi High Court, a creator's verified account with about 1,03,000 followers was withheld across India on the basis of a single-page, system-generated notice from a State police CID which named no post and no complainant. On 18 September Instagram restricted a post by the Software Freedom Law Centre which discussed the removal of Alt News' fact-checks. A reel on the proposed data centre in Visakhapatnam, which IFF also challenged, was restored this week after three and a half months, after the blocking order obtained in litigation turned out to allege "misinformation" about a person who does not appear in the reel. It is also worth recording that this has taken place in the weeks after Meta, having removed a post by the Prime Minister and been given three days by a parliamentary committee to apologise, sent its chief global affairs officer to Delhi to do so.

The case of the journalist Ila Kazmi shows how the system works when it is directed at reporting on the police themselves. On 23 July she published a two-part report on her Instagram account @ ilareports showing police personnel seated in a van at Jantar Mantar and matching live CCTV footage against photographs of individuals. This was the first public documentation of facial recognition being used at the protest, and IFF relied on it when it wrote to the Commissioner of Police and filed RTIs. Part 2 of the report was restricted in India on 24 July under a Section 79(3)(b) notice. On 4 September she posted a reel referring to The Indian Express's investigation into the list of 2,873 persons which the Delhi Police told the Supreme Court its facial recognition system had flagged at the protest. By the police's own preliminary assessment, 162 people on that list were lodged in prison at the time. On 9 September her entire account was withheld in India, again citing Section 79(3)(b), even as the Account Status page on the same app informed her that her account "meets all of our guidelines". She wrote to MeitY. On 15 September the Section 69A Cell of the Ministry replied that the account "is blocked under section 79(3)(b) of the IT act" and that she was "requested to take up the matter with the concerned State department". The reply does not say which State or which department. The Union ministry which administers the blocking framework has confirmed to a journalist that her account has been blocked and has declined to tell her by whom. IFF is assisting her.

Most of the people who have written to us are not employed by news organisations. They are students, freelancers and people who run one account with a few thousand followers, in some cases a lakh. They have no lawyers and no way of reaching Meta other than an in-app form which produces the same message each time. When such an account is withheld its audience disappears at once. When its owner receives an email of the kind described above, they do not know what it is or what will follow from it. It is these accounts, more than the larger outlets, which have borne the removals since July and which are now being asked to give up their identities.

IFF condemns the demand for the identities of persons who documented, satirised or commented on a public protest, and the removal of the record they created. We call on the Delhi Police to withdraw the notices and on Meta to decline to act on them and to restore the content.

On the law, there is no investigation for these notices to serve. 

On 1 September 2026, on the application of the Delhi Police itself, the Supreme Court invoked Article 142 to quash all thirteen FIRs registered in Delhi over the protests of 20 to 25 July "along with any proceedings arising therefrom". It directed that any other FIR concerning the same incidents "shall not be pursued or investigated" and shall be "taken to have been closed for all intents and purposes", and it barred the registration of any fresh FIR save one against 2,873 named individuals, confined to allegations of bodily harm and destruction of public property. 

The order records the acknowledgement of the Union and the States that "mere participation in the protests is not taken as an offence under the penal laws", and it makes the relief conditional on both sides honouring the commitments made before the Court. A notice served on an intermediary under Section 94 of the BNSS or Rule 3(1)(j) of the IT Rules is a step in an investigation, and it must be tied to one which the law permits. The Delhi Police is not the investigating agency in any of the thirteen quashed FIRs, which suggests that these requests arise from a separate FIR concerning posts about the Prime Minister. That FIR concerns the same incidents and stands closed by the order. 

In any event defamation under Section 356 of the BNS is a non-cognisable offence, and a court may take cognisance of it only on the complaint of the person aggrieved under Section 222 of the BNSS. The police have no power to investigate it of their own motion, let alone to collect the identities of those who may have committed it.

Our demands

1. The Delhi Police must withdraw every notice issued to an intermediary seeking the identity or subscriber details of any person in connection with content about the protests of 20 to 25 July 2026, and must disclose the FIR, the provision and the officer under whose authority each such notice was issued.

2. The Ministry of Home Affairs and MeitY must publish every notice issued under Section 79(3)(b) concerning content about the protests since 20 July, withdraw those directed at satire, commentary and documentation, and inform every affected person of the agency which issued the notice against them, beginning with the account @ ilareports

3. Meta must decline to act on legal process which, on the face of the Supreme Court's orders of 28 July and 1 September, has no lawful investigation behind it. It must supply to each user it has notified a copy of the process served on it. It must restore the posts, reels and accounts restricted in India since 20 July, inform each affected user of the agency and the ground on which the restriction was imposed, stop applying community standards to documentation of protests and police action, and publish figures for the notices and data requests it has received from Indian authorities since July.

4. The surveillance of protestors, through facial recognition at the site and through requests for data from intermediaries afterwards, must be placed before the Supreme Court and the HPEC. IFF will assist affected persons in doing so.

Any person who has received such an email from Meta, or whose posts, reels or account have been removed or withheld in India, can write to us at legal@internetfreedom.in. We are providing assistance on a pro bono basis.

text:
Most of you want to know what all transpired in between the ‘account withheld in India’ and the final restoration of my account. 

So here’s a quick summary. Please share so that others can take the same recourse, if need be, coz the govt seems in no mood to spare any content critical of it.

On 19th March at 12:23 AM my account was withheld in India.

Very next day, I had a conversation with @SupriyaShrinate and she told me that 12 other accounts met the same fate. She did a live session and addressed media the very same day. That highlighted the issue. The wire, Quint and alt news reported the news.

I swiftly responded to MeitY on 19th March at 4:16 AM enquiring the cause that led to this removal under section 69A. ( Haven’t received any response yet )

Next I consulted with @NakulGandhi511 upon the recommendation of @iArpitSpeaks as he had earlier met with similar fate and got his account back.

Nakul sir guided me for a week and introduced me with @apar1984 who runs @internetfreedom . 

He took over my case pro bono ( for free ) and guided me accordingly. 

On 1st of April I finally filed my writ petition. The notary, wakalatnama was all new to me coz I had never been in court till this date but barring that I had to do nothing. 

Every response, every draft was given to me by @namanbasoyaa who works with Apar sir. 

I got my listing on 6th of April with the honr Judge Purushaindra Kumar Kaurav. 

He didn’t even waste 10 mins and ordered a restore provided that the posts that warranted an action against me shall stay unblocked until the committee level hearing of MeitY ( It’s not scheduled yet )

In fact I still don’t have the blocking order that necessitated such an action against me that is ultra vires of the constitution. Section 69A doesn’t permit govt to remove pre-emotive post based on speculation and that’s exactly what govt effectively did by withholding my entire account not some posts. 

Also big thanks to my followers who stood with me. Some used VPN just to stay connected. I’m indebted to all of you and IFF and Apar sir in particular. 

Taking this opportunity to urge the govt to remove ban from other accounts as well folllwing the same precedence used in mine and @DrNimoYadav ’s case.

FoS needs to be supreme. Taking down post is wrong in itself but an entire account that took years of cultivating is just brutal and uncalled for. 

May better sense prevails. Peace ✌🏽

Dear @raghav_chadha ,

I know you are doing very well in Parliament by raising small issues that were ignored by most Members of Parliament but have a bigger impact.

I am writing this post regarding an account lien and bank freeze by the Cyber Police of India.

In my case, the issue started when I received a message from my bank branch stating that my account had received a police notice of lien of 6000 rupees. I immediately went to my bank branch and asked them why my account had a lien of 6000 rupees. They followed some procedure and gave me a printout which contained the acknowledgement of my lien. One of the bank employees told me that I should contact the cyber police mentioned on the paper and provide them with the details of the 6000 rupees, such as where it came from and for what reason. However, they did not give me any specific reason why my bank account had received the lien.

Later, I checked my bank statement to find the details of the 6000 rupees transaction and noticed that my case was reported on 6 December 2025, and I had received a transaction of 6000 rupees on the same date. I remember that my neighbour had sent me this 6000 rupees and asked me to withdraw it from the ATM because he had an urgent situation as his mother was going to her village due to an emergency. As a friend, I withdrew the money and gave it to him.

Now I have all the proofs and details to explain to the police, so I emailed all the details to the Bangalore Cyber Cell or the police station where my notice was issued, as mentioned in the acknowledgement given by my bank. However, I did not receive any response. I then tried to contact the investigation officer mentioned in the report. I called several times, keeping a gap of five to six hours out of respect for his time and duties, as they may have many other responsibilities. I also sent him a message on WhatsApp, but there was still no response.

After four to five days, I called again, and this time he picked up the call. He was speaking in the local language, which I did not understand, as I am from Maharashtra and not familiar with the local language of Bangalore. I then started speaking in English, and he told me that I have to come to Bangalore and verify my documents. I explained that for 6000 rupees, it would not be beneficial for me to travel to Bangalore because transportation, food, and stay would cost more than 6000 rupees. He said that he does not know and that I have to come, otherwise he will not issue the No Objection Certificate, and then he ended the call.

This issue may look small, but similar issues are happening everywhere, and no one is noticing them. It feels like “Kare koi aur bhare koi.” Many innocent people face this issue, and it remains unresolved. Because of chain transactions that come into accounts, some people are unable to use their own money. If I travel, I will have to spend more than 6000 rupees to remove the lien. I believe this issue can be resolved through email or online verification, but the investigation officer denied it.

I am also tagging Pushpendra Sir @pushpendrakum and Bangalore Cyber Police @BlrCityPolice . If you could please look into this matter.

Thank you.

Bhai aur beheno, agar aap bhi Binance P2P trading karte ho aur suddenly bank account freeze ho gaya hai toh pareshan mat ho. Yeh bahut common problem hai India mein. Innocent log bhi fas jaate hain jab kisi buyer/seller ka paisa kisi fraud case se link hota hai.

Yeh steps follow karo - 

1️⃣ Sabse Pehle Bank Branch Jaao  
   - Freeze ka exact reason, Cyber Crime complaint number, IO naam aur Police Station details lo.  
   - Written notice maang lo.

2️⃣ Saare Proofs Collect Karo (Bahut Important)  
   - Binance P2P complete order history (screenshots)  
   - Buyer/Seller ke saath chat  
   - Payment proof (UPI, bank transfer screenshot)  
   - Bank statement jisme transaction dikhe  
   - Aadhaar, PAN, Binance account details

3️⃣ Binance Support ko turant contact karo  
   - App mein Help section → Submit ticket  
   - Order ID aur proofs attach karo. Woh counterparty ko investigate kar sakte hain.

4️⃣ Cyber Cell mein Representation Daalo  
   - Local Cyber Police Station ya online portal pe jaao.  
   - Detailed application likho ki transaction genuine tha Binance P2P pe hua.  
   - Saare proofs attach karo.  
   - Lawyer (Cyber crime specialist) ki madad le lo - yeh bahut kaam aata hai.

5️⃣ Follow-up karte raho

This sparked a political row, followed by police-directed efforts to remove related social media posts

This takedown action itself became controversial, with critics framing it as an attempt to suppress discussion of an official lapse during an election period, while authorities maintained it was necessary to stop the circulation of a withdrawn and erroneous document that was being used to question the ECI’s credibility.The episode remained a flashpoint in the final stretch of the Kerala campaign, with the ECI treating it as a corrected administrative mistake and the opposition presenting it as evidence of deeper concerns about the poll body’s independence.The letter and the seal
The document was an ECI communication dated 19 March 2019 containing guidelines/FAQs on the publicity of candidates’ criminal antecedents (following a Supreme Court judgment). CPI(M) and Congress shared versions online showing the BJP Kerala unit’s seal. It had been circulated by the Kerala CEO’s office to political parties, District Election Officers, and Returning Officers as part of clarifications around mid-March 2026.thesouthfirst.comKerala CEO / ECI explanation:
It was described as a “purely clerical error.” The BJP Kerala unit had approached the CEO’s office seeking clarification on the (by then revised) 2019 guidelines and submitted a photocopy of the original directive that already bore the party’s seal. Staff overlooked this and redistributed that version. The error was identified; on 21 March a formal withdrawal notice was issued telling recipients to disregard the document. An Assistant Section Officer was suspended pending inquiry. Later, a Deputy CEO and a Section Officer were relieved of election-related duties.livemint.comOpposition parties (CPI(M) and Congress) rejected the clerical-error account. They alleged compromised institutional neutrality, claiming seals were being “casually swapped” and questioning whether the ECI and BJP shared the same “power centre.” Some BJP responses labelled the circulation of the old document as misinformation or a political plot.thewire.inDeletion of posts controversyActing on an ECI directive (under the Model Code of Conduct), the Kerala Police cyber cell issued notices to X (Twitter), Facebook, Instagram, and numerous individual accounts. The Special Intensive Revision is not only about checking electoral rolls. It is also a large-scale exercise in collecting, digitising and matching personal data. When the system cannot match an elector to an old database, the burden shifts back to the individual to prove their identity, eligibility and place on the roll. (1/10)

Read more: https://t.co/2iX4uT7GnX

This creates a basic administrative question. If an elector is already on the roll, and the state’s own database or digitisation process fails to establish a match, why should the consequences of that failure fall primarily on the elector? The answer cannot simply be another form or another document. The process must account for errors in the data, the software and the administration itself. (9/10)
